docs.title: One story. Three rooms. No facts left behind.
What the Bayern exam asks you to practise
docs.text:
The Bavarian medical chamber describes three parts: a patient conversation, documentation, and a doctor-to-doctor conversation, with 20 minutes for each. The target is medical German at C1 level. This guide starts simply so the ideas are accessible; completing these exercises is not proof of C1 proficiency. Current BLÄK exam information.

The source book is a 2024 preparation resource. Current chamber instructions take priority for exam arrangements. Our fictional cases are practice variations, not predictions of what your examiner will ask.

docs.title: The empty box is not a normal finding
docs.text: If Palwasha has not asked about vomiting, she cannot write that Herr Weber denies vomiting. A blank in the conversation is a blank in the evidence. Write noch nicht erfragt—not yet asked—where appropriate, then find out. It is less glamorous than inventing a beautiful complete report. It is also much more useful.

docs.title: The patient says it one way. Your colleague needs another.
docs.text: The patient says it one way. Your colleague needs another. · Herr Weber says, “Seit gestern tut mir der Bauch weh”—my tummy has hurt since yesterday. In the patient room, Palwasha uses familiar words. In her note, she makes the timeline precise. In the handover, she keeps it short. The facts should survive the journey. Think of three envelopes with the same message inside, not three rounds of a game of telephone.

docs.title: Turn the story around
docs.text: Turn the story around · Choose an audience. The words change; the evidence does not. The 3D cards are a visual metaphor, not an anatomy model.

docs.title: Three ways to use a case
docs.text:
On your own: cover the English, say a line aloud, then check the meaning.

With a partner: one plays the patient and one the doctor. Swap roles. A third person can listen for whether the summary matches the actual dialogue.

As a team: pick the same case and compare wording. Ask which response sounds clear, respectful and honest. The goal is not to find the person with the fanciest German noun.

docs.title: Progress, without the guilt counter
docs.text: Each case has a Mark practised button. It remembers your choice only in this browser. It does not send answers to a server, grade clinical competence, or decide whether you are exam-ready. You can clear this local record in the practice room. A return visit is revision, not failure.

docs.title: Try one sentence, not a lecture
docs.text:
„Die Luftröhre teilt sich in größere Atemwege, die in die Lungen führen.“

The windpipe divides into larger airways leading into the lungs. Point to the branches as you say it. Then ask what the patient would like explained next. A diagram supports a conversation; it should not become a presentation the person cannot interrupt.

General anatomy checked against NIH: the respiratory system.

docs.title: The word is long. The route is easier.
docs.text: The word is long. The route is easier. · A patient asks where the air goes. Start with the bigger passages, not a wall of abbreviations. Trace the windpipe and the branching airways towards the lungs. The picture is a vocabulary map—not a way to diagnose why someone is breathless.

„Der Harnleiter verbindet die Niere mit der Blase. Die Harnröhre führt von der Blase nach außen.“

If you switch the words, correct yourself calmly. In real conversations, noticing and repairing an error is a strength. The map shows general anatomy; a person's symptoms still need an individual assessment.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Practice misstep · The conversation gets stuck · Practice misstep: Please start with your abdominal pain; that is today’s case. · Better approach · Make room for understanding · Begin with Hanna’s stated concern, clarify what information the letter contains, and use the history structure to organise what follows. If you do not know a term or result, say so and identify how it can be clarified. Practising a framework prepares flexible listening; it does not guarantee an examination topic.

docs.title: The little blue tablet has no surname
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · The little blue tablet has no surname · Jule is excellent at remembering birthdays and hopeless at remembering tablet names. She describes one as blue, one as round, and one as “the one my husband keeps moving.” Her phone contains a photograph of last year’s medication plan, but a prescription changed last month. The learner wants a complete list before the next patient arrives. Guessing from colour would be quick, and wrong with impressive confidence. The useful next step is to find a reliable current source while recording what Jule actually remembers. · Meet your patient · Jule Sommer, 61 · Practise · Reconcile an uncertain medication name against a current source.

docs.text: Practice misstep · The conversation gets stuck · Practice misstep: A blue morning tablet is probably your blood-pressure medicine. · Better approach · Make room for understanding · Record the reported morning use without assigning a drug name. Ask for current packaging or an updated plan, and agree on an appropriate way to clarify the change with the treating practice or pharmacy. Keep the old list visibly dated so it is not silently treated as current.

docs.text: See the communication skill · A medicine list needs a conversation · assets/medicine-review.png · Dr Daniyal and a patient reviewing medicine boxes and blank list sheets. · Fictional teaching illustration with Dr Palwasha / Dr Daniyal. docs.title: The allergy box needs a story
What changed—and why it helps
docs.text: A useful allergy history contains more than a drug name. Different reactions can have different implications, but the patient should not be expected to classify them alone. Careful questioning improves the record while leaving clinical interpretation to an appropriate assessment rather than a memory contest.

docs.title: The allergy box needs a story
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · The allergy box needs a story · Ben points to “penicillin allergy” on an old card. He remembers becoming unwell after a childhood prescription, but his sister remembers a rash and his father remembers “something with the stomach.” Family memory has become a committee, and the committee has not kept minutes. The trainee could repeat the label without questions or dismiss it because the account is vague. Neither move helps. The conversation needs the reaction, its timing, what treatment was needed, and an honest statement of what Ben cannot reliably recall. · Meet your patient · Ben Adler, 40 · Practise · Explore an allergy label without confirming or deleting it prematurely.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Practice misstep · The conversation gets stuck · Practice misstep: If you cannot remember, it was probably not a real allergy. · Better approach · Make room for understanding · Take the existing label seriously and ask Ben what happened in concrete terms. Clarify timing, symptoms and any available records without suggesting an answer. Document the uncertainty and seek appropriate review when needed. Do not remove the label or convert a possible rash into a proven severe reaction.

docs.title: What changed—and why it helps
docs.text: Everyday units are flexible. Asking for a bottle size or a typical week gives a clearer picture than assuming all glasses match. Suspicion in the wording can make people minimise or withdraw, while neutral curiosity makes it easier to discuss an ordinary but sometimes sensitive part of life.

docs.title: One glass, three different sizes
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · One glass, three different sizes · Ralf says he drinks “just a glass” in the evening. On his kitchen shelf, glasses range from a tiny celebration glass to something that could host a goldfish, so the phrase tells the learner less than it seems. He senses judgement and starts explaining how hard he works. The clinician’s task is to ask about the actual drink, amount and pattern without scoring Ralf’s character. A calm explanation of why the question matters can turn an awkward exchange into useful information for his care. · Meet your patient · Ralf Meier, 55 · Practise · Ask about alcohol quantity without moral judgement.

docs.title: Pull up a chair. Listen first.
docs.text: Pull up a chair. Listen first. · Patient · Nur ein Glas abends. Warum fragen Sie so genau? · Only one glass in the evening. Why are you asking so precisely? · Dr Palwasha · Weil Alkohol für Beschwerden und Medikamente wichtig sein kann. Was trinken Sie und wie viel? · Because alcohol can matter for symptoms and medicines. What do you drink, and how much? · Meist Wein, aber die Menge weiß ich nicht genau. · Usually wine, but I do not know the exact amount. · Wie groß ist das Glas, und an wie vielen Tagen trinken Sie? · How large is the glass, and on how many days do you drink? · A routine social history includes alcohol use. docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Practice misstep · The conversation gets stuck · Practice misstep: Only one glass? Are you sure you are being honest? · Better approach · Make room for understanding · Explain the clinical purpose and ask neutral questions about drink type, container size and frequency. Let Ralf estimate rather than forcing a false precise number. Separate the usual pattern from occasional heavier occasions. Record his account as reported and keep your tone the same as for any other history topic.

docs.text: Your turn · How do you clarify “one glass”? · Enter one unit automatically · Ask drink type, size and frequency · Ask whether he is a good driver · Type, size and frequency translate a vague phrase into usable information. Automatically assigning a unit pretends the missing quantity is known. A question about driving changes the subject and may feel accusatory. The immediate task is to understand Ralf’s pattern, not pass a verdict on him.

docs.title: The operation that did not count
What changed—and why it helps
docs.text: People group events by their own experience, not by coding rules. A short day procedure may feel unlike “surgery.” Asking for examples and plain descriptions often reveals relevant history that a broad yes-or-no question misses, while keeping the patient comfortable enough to correct or expand an answer.

docs.title: The operation that did not count
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · The operation that did not count · Aylin says she has never had an operation. Later she mentions “the little camera in my knee” and a day spent at a surgical centre. In her mind an operation means a large incision and several nights in hospital; the knee procedure did not qualify. The trainee almost writes two contradictory entries. This is not a trap and Aylin has not tried to mislead anyone. She is using an everyday category, while the form uses a medical one. A short, respectful clarification can reconcile them. · Meet your patient · Aylin Koch, 38 · Practise · Clarify everyday meanings of surgery and procedures.

Welches Knie war betroffen? · Thank you; procedures like that also matter to us. Which knee was involved? · Das linke, vor ungefähr vier Jahren. · The left one, about four years ago. · Wissen Sie, was dabei gemacht wurde, und gibt es einen Bericht? · Do you know what was done, and is there a report? · Past surgical history before a diagnostic consultation. docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Practice misstep · The conversation gets stuck · Practice misstep: You said no operations, so that answer was incorrect. · Better approach · Make room for understanding · Explain that the history includes smaller and outpatient procedures too. Ask about side, approximate date, reason and what was done, without treating Aylin’s earlier answer as dishonesty. Preserve uncertainty about the exact procedure until a report or reliable account clarifies it. Add the information rather than arguing over labels.

docs.title: Married does not mean someone is home
What changed—and why it helps
docs.text: A household is not automatically a care team. “Has family” can hide distance, disability, work or another dependent person. Specific questions make the plan realistic and prevent Greta from being given instructions that assume someone will appear at her front door simply because a box says married.

docs.title: Married does not mean someone is home
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · Married does not mean someone is home · Greta is married, lives with her husband and answers “yes” when asked whether she has family. The trainee nearly ticks “support available.” Then Greta explains that her husband needs help dressing and cannot manage the stairs. Their daughter lives two hours away and works nights. Greta has a remarkably organised wall calendar, but the calendar cannot lift shopping bags. The task is to ask who can actually help with specific needs, rather than treating a relationship status as a ready-made discharge arrangement. · Meet your patient · Greta Blum, 72 · Practise · Turn social labels into concrete support information.

Distinguish a possible helper from an agreed arrangement. Include her own caring responsibilities in planning and discuss available support with the team rather than promising a service that has not been arranged.

docs.title: A family history with a question mark
What changed—and why it helps
docs.text: Family stories often contain useful clues but incomplete medical vocabulary. Treating a possibility as confirmed can create unnecessary fear and distort later decisions. Acknowledging uncertainty is not dismissing the concern; it shows exactly what needs clarification before a more meaningful discussion can take place.

docs.title: A family history with a question mark
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · A family history with a question mark · Jonas remembers that his father had “something in the bowel.” He was a teenager at the time, and adults discussed it in the kitchen after sending him upstairs. A cousin now calls it cancer; an aunt calls it inflammation. Jonas is worried that either version means the same thing will happen to him. The learner must not select the most dramatic label to make the record sound complete. This conversation needs both factual uncertainty and space for the fear that brought the family story into the room. · Meet your patient · Jonas Krug, 46 · Practise · Attribute uncertain family diagnoses and respond to inherited-risk fears.

Carry the uncertainty into documentation so later risk discussion starts from the actual evidence rather than a guessed label.

What changed—and why it helps
docs.text: The patient may be using a narrower definition of medicine than the clinician. Naming categories repairs the question instead of blaming the answer. A complete list helps the team identify what needs review, while an alarmed reaction can make a person less willing to mention ordinary self-care habits.

docs.title: The tea that escaped the medication list
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · The tea that escaped the medication list · Mina says she takes only her prescribed thyroid medicine. As she searches her bag, a packet of herbal sleep capsules appears beside a vitamin bottle and a folded shopping receipt long enough to qualify as literature. She does not count these as medicines because they come from a shop rather than a doctor. The learner should not laugh at that distinction or declare every supplement dangerous. The job is to invite a complete list, clarify what she uses, and leave interaction assessment to a proper review. · Meet your patient · Mina Weber, 49 · Practise · Include non-prescription and herbal products without blaming the patient.

docs.text: Practice misstep · The conversation gets stuck · Practice misstep: You said only one medicine; why did you hide the others? · Better approach · Make room for understanding · Normalise the wider question by naming examples such as shop-bought tablets, drops, creams and herbal products. Use packaging to identify what Mina takes and clarify frequency. Explain that a complete list supports a sensible review. Do not recommend stopping or combining products before their contents and her situation are assessed.

Respecting approximate memory avoids false precision and leaves room for measurements and clinical assessment to clarify what is happening.

docs.title: Five kilos needs a calendar

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Practice misstep · The conversation gets stuck · Practice misstep: Take both until the next appointment; that covers all possibilities. · Better approach · Make room for understanding · Collect the exact product names, dates of the plans and Sven’s actual recent use. Flag the conflicting instructions and seek prompt clarification from the responsible clinical team before offering a regimen. Keep the discrepancy visible in handover and avoid treating a familiar nickname such as “blood thinner” as sufficient identification.

docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · The dressing change needs a pause button · Marlene becomes quiet when the dressing trolley arrives. Last time the change hurt, but she did not say anything because everyone looked busy. Today she asks whether she can “be brave enough” to finish it. The learner should not turn this into a test of toughness or promise that it will not hurt. A useful conversation establishes what happened before, how she can signal discomfort and which clinical support is needed. docs.title: When saliva will not go down
What changed—and why it helps
docs.text: Priority changes when the person’s condition changes. A complete form cannot compensate for delayed assessment of a potentially serious swallowing obstruction. Short, direct language helps both patient and team understand why the conversation has stopped. Describe what she reports and what you observe, keeping the cause explicitly unconfirmed.

docs.title: The belt is not a laboratory result
What changed—and why it helps
docs.text: Everyday clues can be valuable without being numerical. A tighter belt may prompt further assessment, but it cannot establish an exact weight loss. Keeping estimated, measured and unknown information separate lets the next clinician interpret the story accurately. It also avoids making Nils feel he must produce a precise answer to be believed.

docs.title: The pharmacy in the coat pocket
What changed—and why it helps
docs.text: Patients and clinicians may use the word medicine differently. A simple invitation to include shop-bought tablets often reveals information a yes-or-no question misses. Package names help identify products; they do not establish amounts taken. Curiosity gives a better history than treating the first answer as deliberate concealment.

docs.text: A test answers a question, not every question. Long names can hide this simple idea and leave a person expecting certainty the investigation cannot provide. docs.title: The allergy story interrupted by a phone
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · The allergy story interrupted by a phone · Sara is describing a previous reaction after contrast material when the clinic phone rings. She has mentioned breathing difficulty and emergency treatment, but the substance and timing remain unclear. When the call ends, the interview almost moves straight to her bowel symptoms. Sara holds an old hospital envelope that she has carried through three appointments; each time someone promised to look later. This time the task is to resume the unfinished safety-relevant story, verify what can be verified and make the uncertainty visible to the team. · Meet your patient · Sara Holm, 45 · Practise · Preserve a serious reaction history during interruptions

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Practice misstep · The conversation gets stuck · Practice misstep: Leave the envelope unread and record no known allergies. · Better approach · Make room for understanding · Return explicitly to the interrupted reaction history. Ask about the exposure, symptoms and care received, and review the old record with permission. Record unknown details as unknown while flagging the reported breathing difficulty. Ensure the relevant team considers the history before planning investigations, without deciding that every imaging test is therefore impossible.

docs.title: An urgent appointment is not a diagnosis
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · An urgent appointment is not a diagnosis · Ralf receives an earlier specialist appointment than expected and concludes that someone must already know he has cancer. His daughter has cleared the family calendar; he has quietly cancelled a fishing trip he had been planning for months. The referral is for assessment of symptoms, and no confirmed diagnosis appears in the available information. You need to explain why a prompt investigation can be appropriate while avoiding both the claim that cancer is established and the equally unsupported promise that it is impossible. · Meet your patient · Ralf Henning, 66 · Practise · Explain referral urgency without false certainty

Wir erklären Ihnen, welche Informationen noch fehlen und wie es weitergeht. · Exactly. We will explain what information is still missing and what happens next. · Ralf receives an earlier specialist appointment than expected and concludes that someone must already know he has cancer. docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Practice misstep · The conversation gets stuck · Practice misstep: Confirm cancer from the appointment speed. · Better approach · Make room for understanding · Acknowledge what the accelerated appointment has made Ralf fear. Explain that referral speed reflects a need to investigate, not a confirmed result. Review the actual purpose and next step using the letter. Offer a route for questions and symptom changes, without speculating about hidden findings or guaranteeing the eventual diagnosis.

docs.title: Explain the next step without guessing the result
docs.text: See the communication skill · Explain the next step without guessing the result · assets/test-uncertainty.png · Dr Daniyal talking with a concerned patient about planned investigations, with a closed folder. · Fictional teaching illustration with Dr Palwasha / Dr Daniyal. Explaining the reason for a referral helps separate a sensible precaution from a conclusion. Honesty about uncertainty is not evasiveness when it is paired with a clear account of what will happen next and who will discuss the findings.

docs.title: The packet count is not the day count
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · The packet count is not the day count · Felix says he takes pain medicine occasionally. His calendar shows frequent headaches, but he counts packets rather than days and uses different products depending on which shop is open. A cupboard labelled important things contains both receipts and several half-empty boxes. He is attending a planned headache review, with no acute warning symptoms supplied in the case. You need to clarify actual use and symptom frequency, avoiding blame and avoiding a new medication plan based on the vague word occasionally. · Meet your patient · Felix Braun, 40 · Practise · Ask about headache medicine use by days and products

Dr Daniyal appears as a fictional teaching character.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Practice misstep · The conversation gets stuck · Practice misstep: Accept occasionally as a complete medication history. · Better approach · Make room for understanding · Ask about headache days, medicine-use days, product names and actual amounts, using the calendar and packaging to support recall. Explain that frequent use is relevant to review without asserting that it has caused Felix’s headaches. Bring the verified pattern to the treating clinician. Do not recommend abrupt changes or a replacement regimen from incomplete information.

docs.title: Her father’s scan is not her scan
What changed—and why it helps
docs.text: A previous family experience can make uncertainty feel like a repeat of an old crisis. Acknowledgment helps the person hear the plan, but it does not establish a shared diagnosis. Common symptoms still deserve individual assessment. The useful promise is a clear explanation of the reasoning and next step, not a result nobody has obtained.

docs.text: A memory gap and a witness report can coexist without contradiction. The witness may supply valuable details but cannot report Tom’s internal sensations. Attribution keeps each account useful. Estimated duration should remain estimated, especially after a frightening event when a short interval can feel much longer to everyone involved.

docs.title: The missing minute belongs to the witness
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · The missing minute belongs to the witness · Tom is being interviewed after an acute assessment of an episode his partner witnessed at breakfast. He remembers reaching for a cup and then hearing several people say his name. His partner describes stiffening and jerking, but Tom cannot confirm the middle of the event because he does not remember it. The breakfast toast has become the least important unfinished task in the house. Your job is to record both accounts accurately, not persuade Tom to describe movements he did not experience consciously or merge the witness’s estimate with a measured duration. · Meet your patient · Tom Berger, 38 · Practise · Separate recalled experience from witnessed seizure features

May we ask your partner what she observed? · Ja, sie hat den Ablauf gesehen. · Yes, she saw what happened. · Wir trennen Ihre Erinnerung und ihren Bericht und kennzeichnen geschätzte Zeiten. · We will separate your memory and her account and mark estimated times. · Tom is being interviewed after an acute assessment of an episode his partner witnessed at breakfast. docs.title: The difference between said and found
docs.text: FSP Guide · learn one conversation at a time · The difference between said and found · Malte tells you that his right leg feels weak. You have recorded his account but have not yet performed a strength examination. In the handover, the phrase patient reports weakness is about to become right-leg paresis on examination. That small change would create a finding that nobody obtained. Your task is to preserve the distinction, state what remains to be examined and avoid polishing the report into greater certainty. Professional language should make the evidence clearer, not make it sound more impressive than it is. · Meet your patient · Malte Frank, 57 · Practise · Distinguish reported weakness from an examined motor finding

docs.title: The supplied source
docs.text:
FSP in Bayern 2024, second edition, Shamil Gurbanov. Supplied as DOC-20260925-WA0007.pdf, 255 physical pages. The file includes clinical-topic examples, a terminology section, empathy phrases, procedure explanations and examination material.

This is an independent educational guide, not an official edition, endorsement or reproduction of the book. The original PDF and extracted text are not redistributed in the repository. Page references are topic pointers; the new fictional dialogues are not quotations from those pages. Printed page numbers generally equal physical PDF page minus three. Ranges in the table show topic coverage; each individual exercise cites the pages used.

docs.title: Current exam information
docs.text: The Bavarian medical chamber's FSP page describes the current exam structure and requirements. Its procedure rules are a separate official reference. Checked 25 September 2026. We deliberately avoid promising exact exam cases, timings of appointments, or a pass based on this guide.

docs.title: How we treat uncertain or unsafe source wording
docs.text:
We do not repeat blanket assurances that a procedure is painless or risk-free, fixed preparation instructions that ignore the individual plan, or certainty about a diagnosis before assessment. We preserve the communication goal and teach appropriate uncertainty. Emergency scenarios stop the routine script and seek the clinical team. Drug doses and treatment algorithms are outside this guide.

The cases have undergone automated structure checks and editorial review for consistency. They are not independently clinically validated. Qualified German-language and clinical review is recommended before adopting the guide as formal institutional training.

docs.title: Additional fact checks
docs.text:
• The person behind the form · University Hospitals of Leicester: Pregnancy checks before X-ray — Possible pregnancy informs an individual examination decision; necessary X-ray imaging is not categorically forbidden.
  • When the walk gets shorter · NHS: Peripheral arterial disease — Walking-related leg discomfort and rest symptoms can be relevant to arterial disease; history alone does not confirm a diagnosis.
  • When the walk gets shorter · NHS Highland: Vascular guidelines — Sudden pain, coldness and movement or sensory change may indicate acute limb ischaemia requiring urgent specialist assessment; no treatment algorithm is reproduced.
  • When the walk gets shorter · NHS: Venous leg ulcer diagnosis — Arterial circulation assessment is relevant before selecting compression for a leg ulcer.
  • The swollen-leg conversation · NHS: Deep vein thrombosis — New leg pain and swelling can warrant urgent assessment for a possible clot.
  • The swollen-leg conversation · NHS: Pulmonary embolism — Sudden breathlessness and chest pain in a possible clot presentation require urgent assessment; severe symptoms require emergency help.
  • The swollen-leg conversation · Cambridge University Hospitals: Ultrasound scan of leg veins — Venous ultrasound assesses for clots and helps inform treatment planning; the case avoids an absolute comfort or result promise.
  • More than a dressing · NHS: Venous leg ulcer diagnosis — Assessment of arterial blood supply is relevant before choosing compression.
  • More than a dressing · NHS: Venous leg ulcer treatment — Wound and compression care need appropriately trained clinical staff; the cases do not teach a dressing or bandaging protocol.
  • More than a dressing · NHS: Sudden confusion — New confusion warrants urgent assessment rather than being treated as routine follow-up.
  • When every clear sentence counts · NHS: Heart attack — Ongoing chest pressure with radiation or associated concerning symptoms can require emergency assessment. The cases teach escalation rather than drug treatment.
  • When every clear sentence counts · NHS: Electrocardiogram — An ECG records cardiac electrical activity; explaining that purpose is distinct from interpreting its result.
  • The stairs tell a story · NHS: Heart failure — Breathlessness during activity or lying down, swelling and weight changes can be relevant. Heart failure does not mean the heart has stopped. These are prompts for assessment, not diagnostic rules.
  • The stairs tell a story · NHS England: Managing heart failure at home — Individual care planning and communication about changing symptoms matter; the guide does not prescribe a universal fluid limit or medication schedule.
  • Coughs with a backstory · NHS: Pneumonia — Respiratory illness may involve cough, fever and breathlessness; severe breathing difficulty requires urgent help.
  • Coughs with a backstory · NHS: Tonsillitis — Inability to swallow and breathing difficulty during a severe throat illness are warning symptoms requiring emergency assessment.
  • Coughs with a backstory · NICE NG120: Acute cough evidence summary — Green sputum alone did not identify an acute-cough subgroup more likely to benefit from antibiotics in the cited evidence; the case therefore avoids colour-only prescribing.
  • A little more breathing room · NHS: Asthma — Asthma symptoms can vary and worsen; severe or worsening attacks need urgent help. Regimens differ, so the guide does not teach one colour-based or universal dosing plan.
  • A little more breathing room · NHS: Spirometry — Spirometry involves guided breathing measurements used in lung-function assessment.
  • When dinner becomes difficult · NHS: Symptoms of oesophageal cancer — Swallowing difficulty warrants assessment; symptoms alone do not confirm cancer.
  • When dinner becomes difficult · NHS: Sore throat emergency advice — Inability to swallow or drooling is a reason for emergency assessment, not a routine interview or a trial drink.
  • The stomach has entered the chat · NHS: Stomach ulcer — Coffee-ground or bloody vomit can signal bleeding requiring urgent assessment; upper abdominal symptoms have more than one possible cause.
  • A pain with a timetable · NHS: Gallstones — ERCP targets bile duct stones; gallbladder removal is a different procedure. Pain with jaundice or shivering requires urgent assessment. An incidental gallstone does not automatically require treatment.
  • Let's talk about the awkward bit · NHS: Inflammatory bowel disease — Persistent bowel symptoms and bleeding warrant assessment; severe symptoms may need urgent help. Communication cases do not infer a diagnosis from symptom duration alone.
  • The question nobody wants to ask · NHS: Symptoms of bowel cancer — Changed bowel habit and bleeding warrant assessment but do not alone establish cancer; ongoing heavy rectal bleeding requires emergency help.
  • The body's pace-setter · NHS: Underactive thyroid — Fatigue, cold sensitivity and concentration difficulty can occur with underactive thyroid but need individual assessment.
  • The body's pace-setter · NHS: Overactive thyroid — Palpitations, shaking and heat sensitivity may accompany overactive thyroid; symptoms require assessment rather than an assumption of anxiety. Treatment options need individual specialist discussion.
  • The afternoon that changed quickly · NHS: Low blood sugar — Possible low glucose with impaired responsiveness needs prompt help. Do not give oral food or drink to an unconscious person. Current symptoms require current assessment rather than reassurance from a prior long-term marker.
  • Big words, careful conversations · NHS: Symptoms of Hodgkin lymphoma — Painless swelling and night sweats merit assessment but do not establish a lymphoma diagnosis.
  • Big words, careful conversations · The Christie NHS: Acute myeloid leukaemia — Unexplained bruising and gum bleeding can be features of blood disease and deserve evaluation; the cases do not diagnose leukaemia from symptoms alone.
  • A headache is not a whole history · NHS: Migraine — Sudden extremely severe headache or new acute neurological symptoms require emergency assessment. Light sensitivity can accompany migraine but does not independently confirm it. Headache and medicine-use patterns are relevant to review.
  • Rebuilding the missing minutes · NHS: Epilepsy — A seizure does not automatically establish epilepsy. Repeated events without recovery need emergency help. Pregnancy planning needs specialist medication review; patients should not make independent treatment changes. Driving decisions need individual advice and applicable local requirements, not a generic clearance date.
  • Rebuilding the missing minutes · NICE NG217: Diagnosis and assessment of epilepsy — A normal EEG must not be used by itself to exclude epilepsy.
  • When swallowing hurts · NHS: Tonsillitis — Breathing difficulty with throat symptoms warrants urgent help; treatment should not be assumed from the symptom label alone.
  • The day did not go to plan · NHS: Broken arm or wrist — Injury symptoms need assessment; new sensory complaints should be brought promptly to clinical attention.
  • The day did not go to plan · Kingston and Richmond NHS: After a wrist fracture — Finger movement can coexist with a wrist fracture; it is not a stand-alone exclusion test.
  • Short words in a busy room · NHS: Spleen problems — Symptoms after abdominal injury may appear or worsen later; concerning symptoms require urgent assessment.
  • The backstory matters · Somerset NHS: Cauda equina syndrome — New bladder changes or altered saddle sensation with back symptoms require emergency assessment; the scenarios do not supply a diagnosis or treatment protocol.
  • Follow the waterworks · NHS: Kidney infection — New confusion during an infection-related illness is a reason for emergency help.
  • Inside the big machines · NHS: MRI scan — MRI preparation includes individual screening for implanted devices and anxiety; specialist interpretation follows acquisition.
  • Inside the big machines · NHS: CT scan — CT preparation depends on the examination; prior contrast reactions and pregnancy possibility should be discussed with the team.
  • Inside the big machines · Cambridge University Hospitals: Nuclear medicine — Nuclear medicine uses radioactive tracers and provides examination-specific information.
  • Inside the big machines · Cambridge University Hospitals: PET-CT — Radiation-protection advice may include temporary close-contact precautions; this supports asking the specific service rather than inventing one interval for all tracer studies.
  • Before we begin · NHS: ECG — ECG records cardiac electrical activity.
  • Before we begin · NHS: Echocardiogram — A transthoracic echo uses a probe on the chest to examine the heart.
  • Before we begin · NHS: Gastroscopy — Sedation changes aftercare and transport planning; follow the service instructions.
  • Before we begin · NHS: Colonoscopy — Bowel preparation belongs to the specific endoscopy plan; sedation is not equivalent to an automatic full anaesthetic.
  • Before we begin · NHS: EEG — EEG records electrical brain activity and requires professional interpretation.
  • Before we begin · NHS: Kidney stone treatment — Shock-wave treatment may cause discomfort and may require more than one session; no universal success promise is appropriate.
  • The medicine list has a plot twist · NHS: Anticoagulants — Anticoagulants have bleeding considerations; procedure and dosing questions require individual professional advice.
  • The medicine list has a plot twist · NHS: Herbal medicines — Herbal products should be included when checking potential medicine interactions.
  • May I examine you? · NHS: Consent to treatment — Agreement follows understandable information; a signature alone does not demonstrate understanding.

docs.title: Warm stories. A visible source trail.
docs.text: Warm stories. A visible source trail. · A story can be friendly and still tell you where its ideas came from. Every practice case links its topic to physical pages in the supplied PDF. Names and conversations are newly invented. Additional sources check specific facts; they do not turn these exercises into a clinical protocol.

docs.title: A kinder way to get better
A simple route through the guide
docs.text:
Start with Your first FSP shift, Ask, listen, check, and The person behind the form. Then choose a clinical topic you already understand in your own language. Use the visuals if a word needs a picture. Move to explanations and examinations when you feel ready.

Starter focuses on one clear skill. Building adds ambiguity or an emotional concern. Stretch combines competing needs, uncertainty or a more demanding handover. These are editorial practice levels, not CEFR certification.

docs.title: Keep the humour on the right side of the desk
docs.text: We can smile at a stubborn printer, a coat with its own chair, or the extraordinary length of a German noun. We do not laugh at pain, fear, disability, accents, literacy or a person's body. When a scenario becomes urgent, the jokes stop and the next safe action becomes clear.

docs.title: What the buttons remember
docs.text:
Quiz choices and the timer run in your browser. Practised-case marks use local browser storage, with no login and no backend. They may disappear if you clear site data or change browsers. The practice room has a clear-progress control.

Do not type real patient data into study notes or repository issues. Use invented examples for rehearsal. The stories in this guide are already fictional, so there is no need to bring identifiable records into the exercise.

docs.title: You are learning a skill, not collecting perfect sentences.
docs.text: You are learning a skill, not collecting perfect sentences. · A memorised sentence is a useful starting point. Understanding when to use it is the real work. Read slowly, practise aloud, and keep the patient's meaning intact. A modest sentence that is true beats an impressive sentence with imaginary details.
